title: Attack vectors: email, SMS, voice, and the web
body_md:
## A channel delivers a claim; it does not certify it
An attack vector is the route by which a request reaches you. Email can carry a link or attachment; SMS or a messaging app can push a short instruction; a call can pressure you in real time; a web search, advertisement or QR code can place a page in your path. The same underlying request may move between channels: “your delivery is delayed” by text, “support” by phone, then a payment page. Do not rank channels by invented open rates or assume voice is expensive and therefore rare. The decisive issue is the requested action.

### Read the transition
At each step ask: **Who is making the claim? What do they want me to open, share, install, approve or pay? Where did this address or number come from?** A recognizable sender name, caller ID, logo or search placement is a presentation cue, not an identity check. HTTPS protects a connection to a site; it does not prove the site's operator is the organization you expected. A genuine alert can also arrive by text or email, so deleting every unexpected message is not a complete response if it describes a real account problem.

A safe transition starts outside the incoming message. Open the service's app from your device, type a known address, or call a number from a statement or your own contact book. Then inspect the account or ask the organization whether a request exists. If the request concerns a colleague, use a previously established work directory and the normal approval route. Merely switching from an email to the phone number printed inside that email is not independent verification: the sender supplied both paths.

### Channel-specific limits
Email authentication and spam filters reduce some spoofing, but a compromised legitimate mailbox can still send a harmful request. A text thread can group a spoofed message with real ones. A caller may know your name and account context. Search results and ads can lead to real or fake services. URL inspection is useful, yet a familiar domain can host a compromised page, and mobile displays may hide parts of an address. No visual clue replaces checking the transaction inside a trusted service.

**A repeatable routine:** pause when the requested action changes control, leave the incoming channel, check through a source you chose earlier, then act through the normal service if confirmed. If you already entered data or paid, contact the relevant provider promptly; the response depends on what was exposed.

widget_config.goal: Identify what a message, call or page asks you to do, then verify that action through an independently chosen route.
widget_config.today_action: Choose one important service and save its official app or support contact for future call-backs.
widget_config.scope: General channel and verification principles; NCSC reporting instructions apply to the UK. A channel or polished appearance alone does not prove fraud or safety.

blocks.title: Parcel text moves to a “support” call
blocks.situation: Synthetic: A text claims a parcel needs an address correction at `https://parcel-help.example`. A follow-up caller says the link is safe and asks for a card to pay a tiny fee.
blocks.analysis: The caller and link reinforce the same unverified claim. A real customs or delivery fee is possible, so the fee alone is not proof. Check the actual order or courier app reached independently; do not use the link or callback number supplied in the text.

blocks.title: A real account alert by email
blocks.situation: Synthetic: Your library emails that a reserved book is ready and provides a pickup deadline. The message uses the library name and a link, but asks for no payment or password.
blocks.analysis: This may be genuine. Open the library app or known website and check the reservation there. The verification avoids both a needless visit and blind trust in the link.

blocks.title: Track a request across channels
blocks.setup: A synthetic storage-service warning reaches you while travelling. Work through the same claim as it moves from email to call to web.

steps.prompt: An email says your files will be deleted tonight and offers a “restore” link. First move?

choices.text: Open the known storage app and inspect notices there.
choices.consequence: You see account state without trusting the email link.
choices.explanation: Urgency makes the request worth checking, not worth obeying immediately.

choices.text: Use the restore link because the email includes your name.
choices.explanation: Personal details can be known to an attacker.

steps.prompt: A caller now says they are support and tells you to call the number in the email. How verify?

choices.text: Call the number in the email.
choices.explanation: Changing devices is not enough when the contact source is untrusted.

choices.text: End the call and use the support contact from your own app or saved records.
choices.consequence: The new route is outside the caller’s instructions.
choices.explanation: A number supplied by the same claim is not independent.

steps.prompt: A web search shows a sponsored “storage recovery” result. Which path?

choices.text: Use the app or a previously known address instead.
choices.consequence: You avoid treating ad placement as identity proof.
choices.explanation: A search result is a route to a page, not verification of its owner.

choices.consequence: You may enter credentials into an unrelated page.

steps.prompt: The official app shows normal files and no warning. What now?

choices.text: Follow the email anyway in case the app is late.
choices.consequence: You give the original claim control again.
choices.explanation: A mismatch warrants support through the known route, not the suspicious link.

choices.text: Treat the incoming claim as unconfirmed, report/block it through the provider’s normal route.
choices.consequence: You stop the chain and preserve the real service.
choices.explanation: Account state from the trusted app is stronger evidence than the incoming messages.

blocks.debrief: Replay the channel changes: email, caller and ad can all carry one story. Verification is independent only when the destination or contact comes from your established source.

questions.prompt: A real bank text warns of unusual activity. What is the safest way to resolve it?

choices.text: Ignore every text because banks never send alerts.
choices.explanation: Real services may send alerts; verify independently.

choices.text: Open the bank app you already use and review activity or contact support there.
choices.explanation: This handles a genuine alert without relying on the message link.

questions.prompt: A caller ID displays your clinic’s name. What does that prove?

choices.text: Only what the phone displayed; call back on a known clinic number before sharing data.
choices.explanation: Caller ID can be misleading and may not identify the caller.

choices.text: It proves the caller is the clinic.
choices.explanation: Display names are not identity proof.

questions.prompt: An email and its linked page both show the same logo. Which inference is sound?

choices.text: The match proves the page is official.
They may be controlled by the same sender; check through a separate source.
choices.explanation: Visual agreement across two attacker-supplied surfaces is weak evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is a HTTPS page insufficient evidence that an offer is legitimate?

choices.text: HTTPS protects the connection to that page, not the truth of its claims.
choices.explanation: A scam site can also use HTTPS.
HTTPS can encrypt traffic, but authentication of the business is a different question.
